newsitem.title: UK: Energy watchdog cool to German EMU oil sale plan.
newsitem.headline: Energy watchdog cool to German EMU oil sale plan.

text.p: The West's energy watchdog on Thursday reacted coolly to Germany's plan to sell a big chunk of its emergency oil stocks to plug holes in government finances.

Bonn said it was considering selling 7.3 million tonnes of crude oil, about 20 percent of total strategic reserves, as a way of cutting its budget deficit to meet strict borrowing requirements for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
The International Energy Agency (IEA), representing the world's major industrialised nations, frowned on the proposal.

"The IEA would consider this unfortunate but even if they do sell these stocks Germany would still meet the IEA requirement of 90 days forward cover," a spokesman at the IEA's Paris headquarters said.

The agency, which draws its membership from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), was established in the wake of the 1974 oil price shock to protect consuming nations against price rises.
IEA ministers meeting last month in Paris were warned against complacency in protecting energy security, which the agency said remained its top priority.
But analysts said the German proposal appeared to reflect a more relaxed attitude about supply security at a senior level in Europe's most oil import-dependent economy.

"What is striking is that a country like Germany without any oil of its own feels comfortable enough to get rid of 20-days worth of stock cover," said Peter Bogin at Cambridge Energy Research Associates in Paris.
Under emergency reserve obligations signed in 1975, IEA members are required to hold at least 90 days of net imports and release oil in the event of serious market turmoil.
The IEA said the sale would be of a "significant" proportion, reducing German stocks by about 25 days of forward cover to 95 days.

Germany relies on foreign supplies of crude and refined products like heating oil and gasoline for 97 percent of its oil consumption. Last year, it imported 2.1 million barrels a day (bpd) of crude and about between 650,000 bpd of products.

Oil traders said the sale, if carried out over the remainder of this year and 1998, would add 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude -- equivalent to the output of big North Sea oilfield -- to an already sloppy market.

"It may be expedient for budgetary requirements but even though it's only 100,000 bpd, it's another nail in a bearish coffin," said Russell Hill, senior crude trader in London for Austrian oil company OMV.

World oil prices on Thursday were running at $17.50 a barrel having fallen $7 from near six-year highs in January. Analysts warned that German inventory sales during the summer, when demand is usually weak, could extend the slide.

German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt was quoted by the Handelsblatt business newspaper on Thursday saying the sales could raise about 500 million marks ($290.3 million) a year in both 1997 and 1998.
A decision on whether to proceed with the sale is expected by July 11, when the Bonn cabinet is due to approve a supplementary budget.

Since the collapse of a government plan to reap billions of marks in profits from a revaluation of Bundesbank gold reserves, Bonn has been searching for alternative ways of trimming its budget deficit without raising taxes.
The oil involved, the entire federal government crude reserve, has been stored since 1975 in salt caverns near the northern port of Wilhelmshaven.

Germany's remaining strategic reserves, another 33 million tonnes, are held by a Hamburg-based agency on behalf of German oil companies. EBV reserves can only be released back to the refineries by government order in times of international crisis.
